name: Abdon
title: Judge in Israel from Pirathon
summary: Abdon, son of Hillel from Pirathon, was one of the so-called "minor judges" who led Israel for eight years. He stood out through his unusually large family: forty sons and thirty grandsons, all riding on seventy donkeys – a clear sign of considerable wealth, political influence, and high social standing in Israelite society. Abdon succeeded Elon as judge, and when he died, he was buried in Pirathon in the land of Ephraim, at what is called the hill of Amalek. Although no accounts of military exploits connected with his service have been preserved, the description of his large household testifies to the important administrative and judicial role he fulfilled in Israel during a turbulent period in the nation's history.

versions.summary: Abdon was the eleventh judge in Israel and belonged to the tribe of Ephraim. He judged Israel for eight years and was known for his large family with forty sons and thirty grandsons who all rode donkeys, a sign of wealth and high social status.
versions.title: The Judge from the Tribe of Pirathon
versions.reason: [minor] The title says "Tribe of Pirathon," but Pirathon is a place name, not a tribe. Abdon was from Pirathon in the land of Ephraim. The title should be clarified.; [minor] The phrasing "the eleventh judge" can be debated depending on how one counts the minor judges. Some traditions count differently. Furthermore, it should be clarified that Pirathon was located in the land of Ephraim, not necessarily that Abdon was from the tribe of Ephraim—the text only states he was from Pirathon in the land of Ephraim.; [minor] The third key event ("Eight-year judgeship") and the second ("His large family") both refer to verse 14. The information about the eight-year judgeship is found in verse 14, but it is somewhat redundant to list this as a separate event when it is already covered. Nevertheless, it is acceptable to distinguish them thematically.; [minor] In the event "Eight-year judgeship," it is claimed that he "maintained peace and order in the land." The biblical text only states that he judged Israel for eight years—attributing "peace and order" is an interpretation not directly supported by the text.; [major] Footnotes are missing. The profile should include footnotes covering historical, linguistic, or theological details, such as donkeys as status symbols, Pirathon as a location, the category of "minor judges," or "the hill country of Amalek."

versions.summary: Abdon, son of Hillel from Pirathon, was one of the so-called 'minor judges' in Israel. He judged Israel for eight years. Abdon was known for his large family, with forty sons and thirty grandsons who all rode on donkeys—seventy in total—which testified to considerable wealth and high social status. He was buried in Pirathon in the land of Ephraim, on the hill country of the Amalekites.

versions.summary: Abdon, son of Hillel from Pirathon, was one of the so-called "minor judges" in Israel who judged the people for eight years. He is known for his unusually large family: forty sons and thirty grandsons, all riding on seventy donkeys. This information testifies to considerable wealth, political influence, and high social standing in the Israelite society of that time. Abdon succeeded Elon as judge and was buried at his death in Pirathon in the land of Ephraim, on what is called the hill of the Amalekites. Although the Bible does not tell of military feats connected with Abdon, the description of his large household underscores the important administrative and judicial role he had in Israel.

versions.reason: [minor] The Bible mentions that Abdon had forty sons and thirty grandsons (Judg 12:14). Although we do not know their names, the children field could at least contain a comment or be consistent with the keyEvents description. However, this is difficult to represent with IDs when the names are unknown, so it is acceptable to leave the field empty.; [minor] The event 'Eight-year judgeship' overlaps with information in verse 14, but the actual detail about the eight-year judgeship is found in verse 15, not verse 14. Verse 14 concerns his family and donkeys, while verse 15 states that he judged Israel for eight years, then died and was buried. The reference should be corrected to verse 15.; [minor] The summary is good, but the sentence 'Although the Bible does not tell us about military feats associated with Abdon' uses the word 'Bible' in a generic yet acceptable way. Still, a slight rewording could make the text even more varied from version 2.; [minor] The footnote on 'lesser judges' mentions Shamgar, but many scholars do not count Shamgar among the 'lesser judges' in the traditional sense, since he is mentioned in a different context (Judg 3:31; 5:6). It is more precise to list Tola, Jair, Ibzan, Elon, and Abdon as the five 'lesser judges'.

footnotes.text: The fact that Abdon's sons and grandsons rode on donkeys (Hebrew: עֲיָרִים, ayarim) was a sign of wealth and high social status in ancient Israel. Donkeys were valuable riding animals, and owning seventy of them indicated significant riches and political influence (cf. Judg 5:10; 10:4).

Abdon belongs to the group often called the 'minor judges'—Tola, Jair, Ibzan, Elon, and Abdon—who are mentioned briefly in the Book of Judges without detailed accounts of military exploits. These judges appear to have had primarily administrative and judicial roles, unlike the 'major judges' such as Gideon and Samson, who are characterized by dramatic stories of deliverance.

Pirathon is usually identified with Fara'ta, about 10 km southwest of Nablus (biblical Shechem) in the central highlands. The site lay within the territory of the tribe of Ephraim, placing Abdon in the Israelite heartland.

The expression 'the hill country of the Amalekites' (Judg 12:15) is remarkable, since the Amalekites are usually associated with the Negev desert in the south. This may suggest that a group of Amalekites had settled in the hills of Ephraim, or that the place name preserves an old tradition from a previous conflict with the Amalekites in this area.

The number seventy has symbolic significance in a biblical context and can be linked to completeness and authority. Seventy elders were chosen to assist Moses (Num 11:16), and seventy was also the number of nations listed in Genesis 10. Abdon's seventy descendants riding on donkeys may thus signal an extensive and authoritative leadership role.

The Hebrew name Abdon (עַבְדּוֹן) can be derived from the root עבד (abad), meaning 'to serve'. The name may therefore mean 'servant' or 'one who serves', which fits well with his role as one who served the people through judicial and administrative leadership.
